note: The ONLY place two differently-spelled names may become one person. tools/compile_gazetteer.py keys the gazetteer on the whole normalized name, so nothing coalesces by accident; anything that should coalesce is declared here, with the judgement written out. Three rules the compiler enforces: a merge needs a `merge_rule`; the rule must name BOTH spellings verbatim, so it can be read back without the code; and same surname with different initials NEVER merges, rule or no rule — the 1835 letter lists are full of families and an initial is often the only thing separating two of them.

merges.merge_rule: One woman, one advertisement, two readings of it a week apart. 'Mrs. H. Sherman' is how the milliner's own standing advertisement is set in chicago_democrat_1834_12_03 (claim c016, page 3 column 2), and '[Mrs.] Herman' is how the SAME advertisement — same trade, same 'formerly of White …', same anchor against the Mansion House, same Nov. 25 1834 dateline — was read a week earlier out of the badly cut column of chicago_democrat_1834_11_26 (claim c002). The difference is a dropped initial and a dropped S at the head of the surname, which is recognition-class damage and not a second person: '[Mrs.] Herman' has no independent witness anywhere in the corpus, and no Herman appears in any letter list. This merge is made because the two records are two transcriptions of one line of type; it is NOT made on the strength of the surnames resembling each other, and it would not be made if the December printing did not carry the December 3 advertisement's other three fields unchanged.
